clinicalPearls: Most common and most severe of the primary hyperoxalurias, caused by biallelic AGXT mutations that reduce hepatic peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT) activity.
Oxalate overproduction drives recurrent calcium oxalate urolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis and progressive chronic kidney disease, often reaching end-stage renal failure.
Biochemical signature is markedly raised urinary oxalate together with raised urinary glycolate, distinguishing it from type 2 (L-glycerate) and type 3 (4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate).
A subset, especially those carrying the Gly170Arg variant, are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) responsive with reduced oxalate output, so a supervised trial is worthwhile in all patients.
A distinctive molecular lesion is mistargeting of AGT from the peroxisome into mitochondria, where the otherwise competent enzyme is metabolically ineffective.
Once renal function declines, plasma oxalate rises and systemic oxalosis develops with deposition in bone, myocardium, conduction system, retina, skin, vessels and nerves.
Because the enzyme defect is liver-specific, definitive correction needs the liver; combined or sequential liver-kidney transplantation is considered in advanced disease.
Hepatic RNA interference therapy that lowers glycolate oxidase reduces oxalate precursor supply and has transformed medical management.
reference.pathophysiology: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 is an autosomal recessive inborn error of glyoxylate metabolism caused by deficient activity of the liver-specific peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT), encoded by AGXT and dependent on pyridoxal phosphate as cofactor. AGT normally transaminates glyoxylate to glycine within the peroxisome; when it is deficient, glyoxylate escapes and is oxidised by lactate dehydrogenase to oxalate, a metabolic end-product that humans cannot degrade. The resulting oxalate load is excreted by the kidney, where supersaturation drives calcium oxalate crystallisation, causing recurrent stones, tubulointerstitial injury and nephrocalcinosis. A characteristic molecular abnormality, particularly with the Gly170Arg allele, is mistargeting of catalytically capable AGT away from the peroxisome into mitochondria, where it cannot perform its function. As glomerular filtration falls, plasma oxalate rises and calcium oxalate is deposited throughout the body, including bone, myocardium, the cardiac conduction system, arterial walls, retina, skin and peripheral nerves, producing the multisystem picture of systemic oxalosis.
additionalDifferentials: Enteric (secondary) hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption, short bowel or bariatric surgery
Dietary hyperoxaluria from excessive oxalate or precursor intake
Idiopathic calcium oxalate stone disease with hypercalciuria or hypocitraturia
Dent disease and other hereditary tubulopathies causing nephrocalcinosis
Cystinuria and other monogenic stone-forming disorders
additionalInvestigations: Urinary oxalate and glycolate quantification, age-adjusted and corrected for creatinine in young children
Plasma oxalate measurement, especially as renal function declines
Renal tract ultrasound and imaging for stones and nephrocalcinosis
Molecular genetic testing of AGXT as confirmatory diagnosis, often avoiding biopsy
Echocardiography, ophthalmological review and bone assessment when systemic oxalosis is suspected
Historically, liver biopsy for AGT enzyme activity and subcellular localisation
redFlags: Nephrocalcinosis or recurrent stones in infancy or early childhood with failure to thrive and rapidly falling renal function (infantile oxalosis)
Rising plasma oxalate as GFR declines, heralding systemic oxalosis
New conduction abnormality, cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia suggesting myocardial oxalate deposition
Rapid graft loss after isolated kidney transplantation due to recurrent oxalate deposition
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on genotype, pyridoxine responsiveness and how early treatment begins; untreated disease commonly progresses to end-stage renal failure and systemic oxalosis. Early diagnosis, hyperhydration, crystallisation inhibitors, pyridoxine where effective and modern RNA interference therapy have substantially improved renal and overall outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent childhood stones to common idiopathic stone disease and missing the diagnosis until renal failure
Performing isolated kidney transplantation without addressing the hepatic enzyme defect, leading to rapid oxalate recurrence in the graft
Failing to use intensive fluid and dialysis strategies around transplantation to clear the systemic oxalate burden
Not trialling pyridoxine and thereby missing a responsive subgroup
Interpreting urinary oxalate without correcting for age, body size or renal function
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Paediatric and adult nephrology reference texts
management: RNA-interference therapy such as lumasiran to suppress hepatic oxalate overproduction as the disease-modifying mainstay
Supervised pyridoxine trial, particularly with the Gly170Arg allele, continued long term if urinary oxalate output falls
Aggressive maintenance hyperhydration combined with crystallisation inhibitors such as potassium citrate, orthophosphate and magnesium
Stone clearance and relief of urinary obstruction using nephron-sparing endourological techniques
Intensified dialysis regimens to clear the oxalate load in advanced renal failure, since conventional dialysis is inadequate
Combined or sequential liver-kidney transplantation to correct the hepatic enzyme defect and replace the failed kidneys
Surveillance for systemic oxalosis with echocardiography, ophthalmological review and bone assessment, alongside monitoring of plasma and urinary oxalate and renal function
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive AGXT inheritance
